1.pericope_label: Servants of Christ to the saints at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons
debates: What the greeting to bishops and deacons proves: Henry, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley all take bishop and presbyter as one office in the New Testament, Calvin adds that the later restriction of the name rests on no Scripture authority and let one man usurp dominion over his colleagues, while Ellicott grants the indifferent use of the titles but insists it in no way weakens the second-century development of the Episcopate
Why Paul omits the title of apostle: Chrysostom says he writes to equals and has no injunctions to lay on them, while Clarke holds that his authority was simply not in question at Philippi
outliers: Barnes's refusal to let the battle of Philippi be the reason the town is remembered, since it was the first place in Europe where the gospel was preached

Barnes's report that two American missionaries visited the ruins in May 1834, saw what may have been the market-place where Paul and Silas were beaten, and found the road from Neapolis still paved throughout
Henry's observation that this is the only one of Paul's epistles in which no censure is implied or expressed
themes: the founding of the church at Philippi

3.pericope_label: Thanksgiving, fellowship in the gospel, and the work God will finish
debates: What the fellowship in the gospel is: Barnes canvasses three views and decides for their liberality in supporting it, with Gill agreeing, while Henry argues from Paul's thanksgivings for other churches that it is more generally the fellowship of faith, hope and love

How far the confidence of verse six reaches: Barnes rests it wholly on God having begun the work and denies that man could give any such security, while Robertson insists God will not consummate it without their partnership and Ellicott places man's co-operation in the process between grace at the beginning and grace at the end

When the work is completed: Calvin prefers to carry it past death to the resurrection, since the departed have not yet reached what they aspire to, while Barnes takes the day of Christ as the judgment
outliers: Henry's observation that Paul remembers with joy the very town where he was scourged and put in the stocks, counting his sufferings there his credit and his crown
Wesley's summary of the whole epistle in four words, I rejoice, rejoice ye, and his remark that this letter follows Ephesians as joy follows love

Calvin's distinction between assurance of one's own salvation, which is the inward witness of the Spirit and remains shut up, and the judgment we form of another, which rests only on the outward efficacy of the Spirit

7.pericope_label: Held in the heart: partakers of grace, and the oath of affection
debates: Who holds whom in the heart: Barnes and Ellicott take it that Paul holds the Philippians, Ellicott calling the order and context decisive, while Robertson holds that the Greek cannot decide it and Henry gives both readings

What the shared grace is: Ellicott prefers the marginal reading and identifies it with the grace given to Paul to preach to the Gentiles, while Barnes takes it of the divine favour attending his labours, in which they would share for having stood by him
outliers: Calvin's argument that the confirmation of the gospel cannot rest on the steadfastness of men, since though all men were liars God remains true, but that weak consciences are confirmed by such helps, the martyrs being so many seals by which the gospel is sealed in our hearts
Calvin quoting the saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church, and adding that he had imitated it himself in a Latin poem
Chrysostom's observation that a flatterer would not have called God to witness, since that cannot be done without peril
Ellicott's remark that the parallel adjurations show in what sense the apostle understood the command to swear not at all

9.pericope_label: The prayer: love abounding in knowledge, and the fruits of righteousness
debates: Whether to render approve things that are excellent or try things that differ: Barnes says the margin gives the sense better and Gill follows it, while Ellicott defends the received rendering as carrying the idea of distinctive and relative excellence

What without offence means: Ellicott prefers the sense of giving no offence to others, while Calvin, though allowing the older exposition, prefers the passive sense of not stumbling ourselves as we go forward in our calling

Whether the fruit is righteousness or its product: Ellicott argues from the tense of the participle for the former, while Calvin is chiefly concerned to deny that the presence of such fruits proves righteousness before God
outliers: Clarke's figure of love as a river fed by rain and fresh streams until it floods the adjacent plains, set against Robertson's insistence that the perpetual flood still has banks

Calvin's dismissal of a reading that would make your love a title of address for the Philippians, like your reverence or your paternity, on the ground that no such expression occurs in Paul and such fooleries had not then come into use
Barnes's two derivations for sincerity, what is judged of in sunshine and what is without wax, like honey that is pure and transparent
Wesley's remark that the fire which burned in the apostle never says, it is enough

12.pericope_label: The bonds turned to furtherance: the praetorium and the emboldened brethren
debates: What the praetorium is: Barnes, Clarke and Calvin take it of the emperor's palace, Calvin naming it that of Nero, while Ellicott follows a modern scholar in making it the praetorian guard, a body of men rather than a place, and Robertson agrees while reporting that others argue for the judicial authorities of the imperial court

Why the brethren grew bolder: Barnes canvasses four explanations, including the unflattering one that some seized the chance to set themselves up as preachers, while Henry and Calvin take it wholly as the encouragement drawn from his constancy
outliers: Henry's description of the case as a strange chemistry of Providence, extracting so great a good as the enlargement of the gospel out of so great an evil as the confinement of the apostle

Calvin's charge that we allow Christ crucified to be preached, but when he appears in connection with his cross we are thunderstruck at the novelty and avoid him, and that in the persons of those who bring us the gospel as well as in our own
Barnes on the chain: who would wish to be bound night and day to a living witness of all he did, to a spy on all his movements, never at liberty to be alone
Gill's observation that the bonds were not for debt, which the apostle took care never to run into, nor for any capital crime

15.pericope_label: Preached of envy and of good will, and why either is cause for joy
debates: Who preached of envy: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all identify them as Judaizing teachers and rivals within the church, while Gill insists they were true brethren and members of the church, since Paul owns them as brethren in the ministry and rejoices in their preaching

What not sincerely means: Ellicott says the rendering misleads, the word being not purely, and that no hypocrisy is charged but an admixture of partisanship, and Calvin argues from the context that the fault lay in the mind and not in the doctrine taught

How they added affliction to his bonds: Barnes calls the question unanswerable and conjecture useless, while Ellicott adopts the ancient view that they worked on his keepers to increase his confinement
outliers: Calvin's answer to why men would persecute a doctrine they themselves approve, that ambition is blind, nay, it is a furious beast, with his admission that he had seen men in his own day preach the gospel only to gratify the rage of the wicked against pious pastors

Calvin's limit on the rejoicing: God may accomplish an admirable work by depraved instruments, but had the matter been in Paul's hand he would never have ordained such persons, and they are not on that account to be reckoned Christ's lawful ministers
Barnes's rule that even where others preach what we count error we may rejoice, since the most stammering announcement that man has a Saviour may save a soul, whereas ignorance could save none
Chrysostom's image of the lofty soul as a fortress on which nothing in this present life can fix its fangs, neither enmity nor slander nor plots

19.pericope_label: Salvation through their prayers, and to live is Christ
debates: What the salvation of verse nineteen is: Clarke takes it of temporal safety and release, Barnes names him among those he rejects and takes the trials themselves as means of salvation, Ellicott makes it a safety shown either in life or in death, Calvin denies it is bodily safety at all, Wesley reads a higher degree of glory, and Robertson reports both views and asks whether Paul held them together

How to construe to me to live is Christ: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all take Christ as the substance or scope of the life, while Calvin says interpreters have hitherto rendered it wrongly and makes Christ the subject of both clauses, gain in life and in death alike, with Clarke reading it the same way and Henry reporting it
outliers: Ellicott's observation that the apostle uses the first person for the chance of failure, I shall be ashamed, but says Christ shall be magnified for the triumph, since failure could only be his own fault and triumph his Master's strength
Calvin's caution that prayer and the supply of the Spirit, though joined in one clause, are not alike, the supply being the efficient cause and prayer a subordinate help

Barnes's comparison of the singleness with which Paul pursued this aim to that of a miser pursuing gold, with the remark that no believer regrets at death having lived so, though many regret that they did not

22.pericope_label: The strait betwixt two, and the confidence that he would abide
debates: Whether the confidence that he would abide was fulfilled, and what kind of knowledge it was: Clarke states as fact that he was released after two years and Wesley calls it a prophetic notice, while Gill denies there is sufficient proof of the release and makes it conjectural knowledge, Barnes warns that know is not to be pressed, and Ellicott infers a limit to apostolic inspiration itself

How to construe the broken sentence about living in the flesh: Ellicott calls the received rendering inaccurate and perhaps a softening gloss, Robertson notes there is no if in the Greek and suggests I do not declare what I shall choose, and Barnes doubts whether the older rendering can be got out of the Greek at all
outliers: Barnes taking the words for being in a strait from a ship at anchor when violent winds blow that would drive it to sea, his affection for them holding like the moorings while a heavenly influence bore upon him like the gale

Chrysostom's admission that we all shudder at death, some by reason of many sins, of whom he counts himself one, before he presses the apostle with the trader who might run into port, the wrestler who might be crowned, and the general who might refresh himself in the palace
Ellicott's conclusion that the apostolic inspiration, like the apostolic power of miracle, was a gift relative to the apostolic work and did not necessarily extend beyond it
Calvin's rule that the saints hold a sure persuasion only where they have a sure token from God, and expect everything else conditionally

27.pericope_label: Citizens worthy of the gospel, and the gift of suffering
debates: What the evident token is a token by: Ellicott refers it to their fearlessness, Clarke reports critics who refer it to the faith of the gospel itself, and Barnes to the persecution together with the constancy shown under it

Whether affliction can be called a ground of salvation: Calvin insists the word means a proof and not a cause, since Scripture nowhere teaches that the sufferings of the saints cause their salvation, and Henry guards the same point by denying that salvation is to be ascribed to bodily afflictions
outliers: Ellicott's evidence that Christian fearlessness told even on its despisers, since the Stoics spoke of it with affected contempt as a kind of madness, a morbid habit, a sheer obstinacy
Robertson's borrowed line that the Christian gladiator does not anxiously await the signal of life or death from the fickle crowd

Calvin's claim that persecutions are in a manner seals of adoption and that in them God arrays us in his livery, followed at once by his complaint that more will be found to bid God retire with such gifts than to embrace them
Henry's rule that it is not simply the suffering, but the cause, and not only the cause but the spirit, which makes the martyr
